name: Light Celandine Green
lede: Light Celandine Green is a pale grey-green from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, filed as a named color in the 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary, and close enough on screen to Morning Blue to pass for the same color.

sections.title: A Ridgway tone, named again in 1955
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* carries this swatch on plate XLVII, hue 33″″″″, tone d [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary files the exact name "Light Celandine Green" under block 154, "brilliant yellowish green" [2]. The name itself builds the modifier "light" onto [[celandine-green]], the plant-named color rather than a word chosen for its own associations [1].

In our color library its closest neighbor is [[morning-blue]], about 3.0 units away, close enough that most viewers would call the two the same color [3]. [[gnaphalium-green]] sits 4.1 units off and greener, and [[bluish-green]] 4.7 units off, greener and lighter still [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive of 23,781 paintings matches this tone in 438 of them, about 1.84 percent, as photographed, more common than 75 percent of the named colors we track [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 29 of the 1,674 paintings from that decade, 1.7 times the rate its museums' own baseline would predict [4].

Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 45 percent of its 259 clearly-ranked appearances [4]. Camille Pissarro favors it most, in 5 of his 50 works in the archive, 4.1 times his museums' baseline rate, and the tone is most over-represented in France, 2.1 times the expected rate [4]. It shares canvases with Pale Olive Grey far more than chance, a lift of 6.5 [4]. The earliest dated match is 1301, 611 years before the name's first 1912 record, so this is a look-alike hue in an old photograph, not proof of the name's age [4]. The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first.
